body:
Why using more fertiliser is not always better

A crop can grow well only when its essential requirements are met in suitable proportions. Excessive application of one nutrient cannot compensate for a severe shortage of another. A field supplied with abundant nitrogen may still produce a poor crop if phosphorus, potassium, water or another essential requirement is limiting.

Fertiliser management therefore concerns the right nutrient, suitable amount, appropriate time and effective application method, rather than simply maximising the quantity applied.

Important consequences of unbalanced fertilisation

Nutrient deficiency

Insufficient nitrogen can restrict vegetative growth, while phosphorus deficiency can affect root development and normal growth. However, visible symptoms should be interpreted carefully because nutrient disorders can resemble disease or water stress.

Nutrient losses and water pollution

Excess nutrients may move away from the crop root zone. Nitrate is relatively mobile in soil and may be leached into water. Phosphorus can also reach surface waters through runoff and erosion.

When excessive nutrients enter lakes and other water bodies, they may encourage abnormal algal growth and contribute to eutrophication, a process associated with deterioration of water quality and oxygen depletion.

Decline in soil quality

Long-term nutrient management that ignores organic matter and soil conditions may reduce soil quality. Organic manure can improve soil structure, aeration and water retention, while appropriately used mineral fertilisers supply nutrients needed for productive farming.

The scientific objective is not to classify all chemical fertilisers as harmful or all organic materials as sufficient by themselves. It is to maintain soil fertility while minimising avoidable losses.

Integrated nutrient management

Integrated nutrient management combines appropriate mineral fertilisers, organic materials and biological nutrient sources to support crop growth and maintain soil fertility over time.

Each input contributes something different:

  • Mineral fertilisers: Supply measured quantities of nutrients such as N, P and K.
  • Organic manure: Adds organic matter and contributes nutrients as decomposition proceeds.
  • Biofertilisers: Use beneficial microorganisms to increase nutrient supply or availability.
  • Nano fertilisers: May provide targeted supplementary nutrients under appropriate crop and soil conditions.

These inputs are often complementary rather than mutually exclusive. For example, applying a suitable Rhizobium inoculant to a legume does not automatically eliminate the crop's phosphorus requirement.

Soil testing and the Soil Health Card approach

A soil test provides information about selected soil properties and available nutrients. India's Soil Health Card initiative is associated with communicating soil nutrient status and recommendations for balanced nutrient use.

Soil-test information helps distinguish a genuine nutrient deficiency from unnecessary fertiliser application. The actual recommendation must consider the crop, local conditions and relevant agricultural guidance.

Simple field applications of the concepts

SituationRelevant nutrient principleReason
Legume grown in a suitable fieldCompatible Rhizobium inoculationSupports symbiotic nitrogen fixation
Flooded rice cultivationCyanobacteria or Azolla-based approachesCan contribute biological nitrogen
Soil with poorly available phosphorusSuitable phosphorus management and PSBSupports phosphorus supply and availability
Crop requiring supplementary nitrogenAppropriate nitrogen applicationSupplies the nutrient actually required
Soil low in organic matterCompost or other suitable manureHelps improve soil organic matter and structure

These examples identify the relevant principle, not an automatic prescription. Product suitability and application requirements remain crop-specific.

How nano fertilisers fit into balanced management

The Department of Fertilisers reported on 20 March 2026 that selected trials achieved satisfactory results with partial substitution of conventional fertilisers. The same report recognised inconsistent results and nutrient deficiencies under some higher-substitution conditions.

This evidence supports a conditional approach: nano products may be useful components of nutrient management, but adequate basal nutrition and soil fertility must not be ignored.

Prelims focus

  • Integrated nutrient management combines mineral, organic and biological nutrient sources.
  • Soil testing helps identify nutrient needs and prevent unnecessary application.
  • Manure contributes organic matter as well as nutrients.
  • Excess nutrient runoff can contribute to eutrophication.
  • Biofertilisers and nano fertilisers act through different mechanisms.
  • Trap: Applying more nitrogen does not automatically correct phosphorus or potassium deficiency.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 1, Crop Production and Management, section 1.5, pp. 5–7, 2018–19 reprint; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 15, Improvement in Food Resources, section 15.1.2(i), pp. 205–207, 2018–19 reprint; Department of Fertilisers, Press Information Bureau, Government Highlights Significant Progress in Nano-Fertilizer Adoption and Drone-Led Agricultural Transformation, 20 March 2026, release 2242958; Government of India, Soil Health Card programme information, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A crop and soil assessment guides N, P and K supply, four distinct input roles, and reassessment in a repeating decision cycle.
pictures.caption: Balanced nutrition requires decisions based on the crop and soil, not on product names alone.

title: Balanced Fertiliser Use, Integrated Nutrient Management and Environmental Effects

body:
India's nano fertiliser development and Gujarat connection

India has promoted nano fertilisers as part of its efforts to improve nutrient-use efficiency and reduce unnecessary fertiliser consumption. An important manufacturing centre is Kalol in Gandhinagar district, Gujarat, where the Indian Farmers Fertiliser Cooperative Limited (IFFCO) has developed nano fertiliser production facilities.

According to the Department of Fertilisers' 2022 year-end review, commercial production of IFFCO Nano Urea at Kalol commenced on 1 August 2021.

On 24 October 2023, IFFCO's Nano DAP (Liquid) manufacturing plant at Kalol was inaugurated. These are historical events whose dates do not change with subsequent alterations in production or sales.

Fertiliser regulation and notified products

The Fertiliser (Control) Order, 1985, commonly abbreviated as FCO, provides the regulatory framework for specified fertiliser products in India. Notifications under this framework identify approved or notified product specifications.

For example, IFFCO Nano Urea Plus containing 16% nitrogen was notified on 15 April 2024, under notification S.O. 1718(E). It also reported the notification of other nano nitrogen products with different nitrogen concentrations.

A product's inclusion in the regulatory framework does not establish that it will produce identical crop responses in all soils or that conventional fertilisers can be completely discontinued.

Important programmes and institutions

Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samriddhi Kendras

Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samriddhi Kendras (PMKSKs) are agricultural-input service and retail centres. The Department of Fertilisers reported on 4 August 2026 that companies were making Nano Urea and Nano DAP available through these centres.

Government promotion also included farmer demonstrations, awareness activities, battery-operated sprayers, drone spraying services and collaboration with agricultural research institutions.

PM-PRANAM

PM-PRANAM stands for the PM Programme for Restoration, Awareness Generation, Nourishment, and Amelioration of Mother-Earth. The programme was approved on 28 June 2023.

It is intended to encourage States and Union Territories to reduce chemical fertiliser consumption relative to their previous 3-year average. Under the reported framework, the incentive is linked to 50% of the fertiliser subsidy saved through the reduction.

PM-PRANAM primarily incentivises States and Union Territories. It should not be confused with a scheme that automatically pays each farmer 50% of the price of a nano fertiliser bottle.

Nano fertiliser field demonstrations

The Department of Fertilisers reported on 27 March 2026 that a Nano DAP promotion campaign, described as a Maha Abhiyan, covered all 15 agro-climatic zones through consultations and field demonstrations.

The same announcement described field-level demonstrations of Nano Urea Plus in 100 districts. These were programme details reported at that date, rather than permanent scientific characteristics of the products.

Gujarat's reported subsidy initiative

In a release dated 4 August 2026, the Department of Fertilisers stated that the Government of Gujarat provided a 50% subsidy on nano fertilisers under a special support initiative.

This is a dated report of a state support measure. Eligibility, administrative conditions and continuation of an incentive can change. The statement should not be extended into a claim that every nano fertiliser purchase remains subsidised at the same rate indefinitely.

Distinguishing the principal organisations

  • IFFCO: An Indian farmers' fertiliser cooperative associated with the Kalol nano fertiliser facilities and products.
  • Department of Fertilisers: A central government department concerned with fertiliser policy and supply-related initiatives.
  • ICAR: The Indian Council of Agricultural Research, whose institutions participate in agricultural research and field evaluation.
  • Krishi Vigyan Kendras: Agricultural extension institutions that help demonstrate technologies and communicate scientific practices to farmers.

One-glance conceptual synthesis

The most important distinction across this subtopic is the way each input contributes to crop nutrition. Conventional urea supplies concentrated nitrogen; conventional DAP supplies nitrogen and phosphorus; nano urea and Nano DAP use specialised formulations to deliver particular nutrients; manure contributes nutrients and organic matter; and biofertilisers employ beneficial living organisms to improve nutrient supply or availability.

These approaches can be complementary, but none should be treated as a universal solution for all nutrient requirements.

Prelims focus

  • Commercial production of IFFCO Nano Urea began at Kalol, Gujarat, on 1 August 2021.
  • IFFCO's Nano DAP (Liquid) plant at Kalol was inaugurated on 24 October 2023.
  • The Fertiliser (Control) Order is associated with 1985.
  • PM-PRANAM was approved on 28 June 2023 and incentivises States and Union Territories for reducing fertiliser consumption.
  • On 4 August 2026, the Government of India reported Gujarat's 50% nano fertiliser subsidy initiative.
  • Trap: A state subsidy percentage, a product's nitrogen percentage and a percentage reduction in conventional fertiliser use describe 3 different things.

[Sources: Department of Fertilisers, Press Information Bureau, Year-end Review of the Department of Fertilisers, 23 December 2022, Innovation Division, release 1886054; Ministry of Cooperation, Press Information Bureau, inauguration of IFFCO Nano DAP (Liquid) plant at Kalol, 24 October 2023, release 1970561; Department of Fertilisers, Press Information Bureau, Import and Sale of DAP, 8 August 2025, release 2154208; Department of Fertilisers, Press Information Bureau, PM-PRANAM Launched to Promote Sustainable Fertilizer Use and Restore Soil Health Across States, 27 March 2026, release 2246007; Department of Fertilisers, Press Information Bureau, Government Intensifies Promotion of Nano Fertilizers to Enhance Nutrient Use Efficiency and Strengthen Self-Reliance, 4 August 2026, release 2294682. Online sources consulted 3 November 2026.]
